extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science and law; legislators and jurists
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of prescriptive and explanatory principles about the role of the legal profession, the jury, laws, manners, and physical/geographical causes in establishing and maintaining a democratic republic (as argued in Tocqueville's Democracy in America).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawyers' influence on civil law
rubrics_metrics.description: In matters of civil law the majority is obliged to defer to the authority of the legal profession, and American lawyers are disinclined to innovate when left to their own choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The legal spirit extends beyond courts because lawyers occupy public stations (legislatures, administration) and thus exercise powerful influence upon formation and execution of law; this conservatism explains why political innovations were adopted more readily than changes to civil law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury as a political institution (sovereignty of the people)
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury is pre-eminently a political institution and must be regarded as one form of the sovereignty of the people; when that sovereignty is repudiated, the jury must be rejected or adapted to the laws by which sovereignty is established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville insists we view trial by jury not merely judicially but politically — it places direction of society in hands of the governed and operates like an instrument of popular sovereignty rather than a mere adjudicative mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualification of jurors aligned with electors
rubrics_metrics.description: The list of citizens qualified to serve on juries must increase and diminish with the list of electors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the jury is a portion of the nation entrusted with execution of the laws (analogous to houses of parliament making the laws), its composition should reflect the political franchise to maintain consistency and uniformity in governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury composition determines aristocratic vs democratic character
rubrics_metrics.description: The institution of the jury may be aristocratic or democratic according to the class of society from which the jurors are selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in England juries are returned from the aristocratic portion of the nation, yielding an aristocratic republic; in the United States juries are drawn from the whole people, reflecting universal suffrage and contributing to the supremacy of the majority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of jury to civil causes strengthens democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: When the influence of the jury is extended to civil causes its application is constantly palpable, it affects all interests of the community, penetrates usages of life, and becomes associated with the idea of justice itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil juries communicate the spirit of the judges to all citizens, teach equity, instill civic responsibility, and serve as a durable bulwark for republican institutions—far more secure when applied to civil matters than when confined to criminal cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury as public school that forms public judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury contributes most powerfully to form the judgment and to increase the natural intelligence of a people; it may be regarded as a gratuitous public school in which every juror learns to exercise his rights and becomes practically acquainted with the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Through direct contact with bar, judges, and legal proceedings jurors acquire political good sense and practical intelligence; Tocqueville credits much of Americans' practical intelligence to long use of the jury in civil cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge's guiding role in civil jury trials
rubrics_metrics.description: In civil causes the judge appears as a disinterested arbiter whose influence upon the jury's verdict is almost unlimited; the jury often sanctions the decisions of the judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many civil questions are not mere factual questions, the judge sums up arguments, directs jurors to the precise question of fact, and in effect puts the answer to the question of law into their mouths; the jury exercises the authority of society while the judge supplies reason and law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury composition and non-responsibility protect innocence
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the people are predisposed to convict, the composition and the non-responsibility of the jury would still afford some chances favorable to the protection of innocence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville notes that the jury's structure can provide safeguards against abuses (e.g., arbitrary power of monarchs) because collective, non-personally-responsible jurors may resist unjust convictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three principal causes maintaining democratic republic
rubrics_metrics.description: All causes which contribute to maintain the democratic republic in the United States are reducible to three heads: I. The peculiar and accidental situation in which Providence has placed the Americans; II. The laws; III. The manners and customs of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tripartite framework structures the chapter: physical/geographical accidents, formal legal institutions, and social habits/customs together explain the stability of American democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical/geographical conditions favorable to democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Accidental or providential circumstances — e.g., the Union has no neighbors, no great metropolis, America an empty country, physical prosperity and wide territory — contribute powerfully to the maintenance of the democratic republic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No neighbors reduces wars and the need for large armies (thus limiting military glory); lack of a dominant metropolis prevents concentration of populace power; a boundless continent and material prosperity make equality and freedom easier to sustain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cities and metropolises as a danger to republicanism
rubrics_metrics.description: The preponderance of capital cities is a serious blow upon the representative system because cities enable concerted, passionate resolutions by a populace which can exercise prodigious influence over magistrates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville warns that large cities (and their particular populations) can threaten democratic republics unless the government creates an armed force independent of town populations to repress urban excesses; he cites contemporary US cities as a potential future danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of settlement and equality of conditions as a foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: The origin of the American settlements — the early settlers' republican condition and customs — was the first and most efficacious cause of the present prosperity and the democratic republic; the forefathers imported equality of conditions into the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond laws and geography, inherited social customs and the initial social structure (chances of birth favoring equality) bequeathed manners and opinions conducive to republican government and long-term democratic stability.
